Break it up
A picture is too big to send in one go. The network cuts it into small numbered packets. Each packet rides its own road, and the numbers put the picture back together at the other end.
Grandma wants a picture of an apple. Send each packet down the road, then rebuild the picture by number.
Where is the packet right now, and which road leaves from there?
The glowing road leads out of the office where the packet is waiting.
Tap the glowing road. When all the pieces have arrived, tap them in order: 1, then 2, then 3.
What does the network do with a big picture before sending it?
Cuts it into numbered packets
Sends it in one giant piece
Prints it on paper first

Two roads lead to the school. Any open road is fine for a packet.

Both glowing roads reach the school in two hops.

Yes, any open road works

Only the first packet may

Many roads
Netville has many roads between its post offices. If one road is closed or busy, a packet simply takes another one. Packets can arrive in any order, so the numbers matter.
Cookies for the school! Watch the roads: one of them is about to close.
A road has closed. Is there another way to the school?
The river road is still open and it is just as short.
Tap the road to the river office, then the road into the school.
A road closes while you are sending. What do you do?
Send the next packets another way
Stop sending forever
Throw the packets away
One office is very busy today. Packets that pass it arrive late, so they may come in a mixed up order.
Why did a later packet arrive before an earlier one?
The busy office (with the clock) holds packets a while. The numbers still tell you the order.
Tap the pieces by number, not by the order they arrived: 1, 2, 3, 4.

Wait, then place them in number order

Send the whole picture again
Roadworks all over town. Two roads will close while you send. Keep finding a way.

Follow the glowing roads: they always show an open way, even if it is one hop longer.
Tap the glowing road each time. The last packet needs four hops instead of three.

So packets still arrive when a road closes
Because roads are cheap

A busy office and a road that closes. Six packets, three hops each, back in order at the end.
Which packets will arrive late, and does that change their numbers?
The busy office slows packets down. A closed road means another road. The numbers never change.
Take the glowing roads, then place the pieces 1 to 6 by their numbers.

This picture is a secret birthday plan. Open roads have a snoopy cat who reads every packet. Sealed roads cost two hops but nobody can peek.
Who can read a packet on an open road?
The roads with the lock are sealed. They cost more hops, but the snoopy cat sees nothing.
Tap the sealed road over the hill, then the sealed road into the house, for every packet.
Why send a secret on a sealed road even if it costs more?
Nobody on the way can read it
It is faster
Sealed roads always arrive first
Say got it
Post offices follow shared rules. When a packet arrives, the house says got it. When a packet is missing, the house asks for that number again. That way nothing stays lost.
Three packets were sent, but the mail van hit a bump. Say got it for each packet that arrived, and ask again for the one that did not.
Which packet number is missing from the board?
Slot 2 is empty. Packets 1 and 3 are waiting for a got it.
Tap packet 1, then Say got it. Tap slot 2, then Send again. Say got it for 2 and 3.

Please send packet 2 again
Nothing, it just waits

Packet 3 came twice. Say got it once, then throw the extra copy away. Slot 2 is empty.
Say got it for 1, 3 and 4. Throw away the second 3. Send again for 2, then say got it.

Rules of the road

A protocol is a set of rules computers agree on before they talk: number every packet, say got it when one arrives, ask again for a missing one, throw away extra copies. Every post office in Netville follows them.
Five packets, two lost on the way. Acknowledge what arrived and ask again for the rest.
Which numbers never reached the house?
Slots 3 and 5 are empty. The sender will only resend what you ask for.
Say got it for 1, 2 and 4. Tap slot 3 and slot 5 and Send again, then say got it for both.
What is a protocol?
Shared rules computers follow to talk
A kind of cable
A very fast packet
A slow got it makes a sender resend too early. Now there are extra copies and one packet is still missing.
Why can the same packet arrive twice?
Packets 1 and 3 each came twice: one got it each, the copies go in the bin. Slot 4 is empty.
Say got it for 2, 1, 3 and 5. Throw away the extra 3 and the extra 1. Send again for 4, then say got it.
Why can a packet arrive twice?
The sender sent it again because the got-it note was slow
The road copied it
Every packet is always sent twice
